title: A retrospective prostate-cancer messaging study finds different strengths in GPT-4 and clinician replies
summary: A retrospective study compared clinical-team replies with a GPT-4-based bot for 158 prostate-cancer patient inquiries. Clinicians rated team replies higher on completeness, correctness and clarity, while bot replies scored higher on empathy and more often required major editing. Four LLM graders favored bot replies and showed lower inter-grader agreement than clinician graders. The reviewed publisher abstract describes an evolving rubric and response-quality evaluation, without establishing patient outcomes, prospective workflow utility or clinical safety effects; full Methods were inaccessible.
ai_technology: GPT-4-based patient-message drafting bot and LLM-based graders
organization: Mayo Clinic; Massachusetts Institute of Technology; Cornell University

evidence.tested: Retrospective comparative assessment of replies to 158 prostate-cancer patient inquiries, using three human evaluation rounds and one LLM-grader round. Clinicians rated team replies higher in completeness, correctness and clarity; the bot higher in empathy; bot replies required major edits more often. LLM graders favored bot replies and showed low agreement (alpha 0.07–0.18) versus clinician graders (0.53–0.81).
evidence.unknown: The article abstract does not establish that patients received the generated replies, any effect on patient outcomes, or prospective clinical utility. Full Methods were not accessible from the Nature article route during this check; the rubric changed across the clinician rounds.
evidence.ai_role: A GPT-4-based bot drafts responses in a specific oncology workflow and LLM graders evaluate the same response set; the study measures concrete strengths and limitations of this AI-assisted communication task.

source_review.scope: Publisher original abstract, publication/acceptance metadata and author affiliations; detailed full Methods not accessible.
